slides.title: Control Types
slides.raw:
Control Types
Preventive
Deterrent
Detective
Corrective
Compensating
Directive
slides.teach: Focus on the differences between the listed types and the clue words that distinguish them in exam questions.

course.learn: Security controls can be classified by what they do: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, or directive. The same technology can sometimes serve more than one function depending on how it is used.
course.why: Security+ scenarios often ask for the BEST control type based on purpose rather than the product name.
course.example: A visible camera can deter a person, while the recorded footage can also be used as a detective control after an event.
course.exam: Focus on the verb in the scenario: stop = preventive, discourage = deterrent, discover = detective, fix = corrective, alternative = compensating, instruct = directive.

breakdown.explanation: Preventive controls are designed to stop a security event before it succeeds. They reduce the chance that an attacker, mistake, or unsafe action can reach the point of causing damage.
Deterrent controls try to discourage a person from attempting an unwanted action. They work by increasing the perceived chance of being caught or the perceived cost of attacking.
Detective controls identify suspicious activity, policy violations, or evidence that an event has occurred. Their value is visibility: they tell defenders that something needs investigation.
Corrective controls reduce damage and restore a system after a problem is discovered. They focus on fixing the condition or returning operations to a known-good state.
A compensating control is an alternative safeguard used when the preferred or required control cannot be implemented exactly as intended.
Directive controls tell people what they are expected or required to do. Policies, procedures, standards, and mandatory training guide behavior.

course.learn: Preventive controls are designed to stop a security event before it succeeds. They reduce the chance that an attacker, mistake, or unsafe action can reach the point of causing damage.
course.why: Prevention reduces the number of incidents defenders have to detect and clean up later, so it is usually the first layer of defense.
course.example: A firewall blocks an unauthorized inbound connection before it reaches a server. MFA can stop a stolen password from being enough to sign in.
course.exam: Look for words such as block, stop, prevent, deny, restrict, or before the incident. Do not confuse preventive controls with detective controls that only alert.

breakdown.explanation: Filter network traffic according to security rules, usually by source, destination, protocol, port, application, or context.
Use hard-to-guess credentials and limit what authenticated users can reach.
Protect readable data by converting it to ciphertext that requires an authorized key to recover.
Teach users how to recognize threats and follow secure behavior so human mistakes are less likely.

defs.definition: Transforms readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key so unauthorized parties cannot understand it.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Preventive and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: Preventive controls are designed to stop a security event before it succeeds. They reduce the chance that an attacker, mistake, or unsafe action can reach the point of causing damage. slides.title: Deterrent
slides.raw:
Deterrent
Security cameras and alarms
Intrusion detection systems
Security awareness posters and messages
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Deterrent controls try to discourage a person from attempting an unwanted action. They work by increasing the perceived chance of being caught or the perceived cost of attacking.
course.why: A control can reduce risk even if it does not physically block an action. Visible monitoring and warning messages can change attacker behavior.
course.example: A clearly visible camera and a warning banner may cause someone to abandon an attempt even though neither one physically prevents the action.
course.exam: If the scenario emphasizes discouraging behavior rather than technically blocking it, deterrent is usually the best answer.

breakdown.explanation: Provide visible deterrence and evidence/notification when physical activity occurs.
Monitor traffic or activity for signs of attack and generate alerts; they do not normally block by themselves.
This contributes to reducing risk in the broader Security Control Types design and should be evaluated as part of defense in depth.

course.check_a: Deterrent controls try to discourage a person from attempting an unwanted action. They work by increasing the perceived chance of being caught or the perceived cost of attacking. Key ideas include: Security cameras and alarms; Intrusion detection systems; Security awareness posters and messages.

slides.title: Detective
slides.raw:
Detective
Log monitoring
Vulnerability
assessments
Antivirus and antimalware software
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Detective controls identify suspicious activity, policy violations, or evidence that an event has occurred. Their value is visibility: they tell defenders that something needs investigation.
course.why: You cannot respond to an incident you never notice. Detection shortens the time an attacker can remain active.
course.example: An IDS generates an alert after identifying malicious network behavior; log monitoring reveals repeated failed sign-ins.
course.exam: Look for alert, identify, monitor, discover, detect, log, or notify. IDS and SIEM are classic detective examples.

breakdown.explanation: Review events from systems and applications to detect suspicious behavior or failures.
Systematically identify and evaluate weaknesses so remediation can be prioritized.
Detect, block, quarantine, or remove malicious software on endpoints.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Detective and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: Detective controls identify suspicious activity, policy violations, or evidence that an event has occurred. Their value is visibility: they tell defenders that something needs investigation. Key ideas include: Log monitoring; Vulnerability assessments; Antivirus and antimalware software.

course.learn: Corrective controls reduce damage and restore a system after a problem is discovered. They focus on fixing the condition or returning operations to a known-good state.
course.why: Even strong preventive controls can fail. Corrective controls make recovery possible and limit the duration of an incident.
course.example: After ransomware is contained, an organization restores clean backups and patches the exploited vulnerability.
course.exam: Look for restore, remediate, recover, repair, remove, or after the incident.

breakdown.explanation: Keep recoverable copies and documented recovery procedures so operations can be restored after disruption.
Keep recoverable copies and documented recovery procedures so operations can be restored after disruption.
Define how an organization prepares for, detects, contains, eradicates, and recovers from security incidents.
Apply vendor updates that fix known security flaws or bugs.

course.check_a: Corrective controls reduce damage and restore a system after a problem is discovered. They focus on fixing the condition or returning operations to a known-good state. Key ideas include: Backups and disaster; recovery plans; Incident response plans; Software patching.

slides.title: Compensating
slides.raw:
Compensating
Manual security reviews
Increased user training
Multi-factor authentication
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: A compensating control is an alternative safeguard used when the preferred or required control cannot be implemented exactly as intended.
course.why: Legacy systems, operational constraints, or cost can make an ideal control impossible. Security still needs another way to reduce the same risk.
course.example: A legacy application cannot support MFA, so access is restricted through a hardened jump server with strong authentication and monitoring.
course.exam: Compensating means alternative control—not a weaker synonym for preventive. The clue is usually that the normal control cannot be used.

breakdown.explanation: This contributes to reducing risk in the broader Security Control Types design and should be evaluated as part of defense in depth.
Within Compensating, this is a specific factor you should be able to recognize and explain. Connect it to the purpose of Security Control Types rather than memorizing the phrase by itself.
Require authentication factors from more than one factor category, reducing dependence on one stolen secret.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Compensating and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: A compensating control is an alternative safeguard used when the preferred or required control cannot be implemented exactly as intended. Key ideas include: Manual security reviews; Increased user training; Multi-factor authentication.

slides.title: Directive
slides.raw:
Directive
Security policies and procedures
Training materials and awareness campaigns
Risk assessments and compliance audits
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Directive controls tell people what they are expected or required to do. Policies, procedures, standards, and mandatory training guide behavior.
course.why: Many security failures come from inconsistent human decisions. Clear direction creates repeatable expectations.
course.example: An acceptable-use policy tells employees which activities are prohibited on company systems.
course.exam: If the control is primarily an instruction, rule, policy, or required procedure, think directive.

breakdown.explanation: Document required security rules and repeatable steps for carrying them out.
Within Directive, this is a specific factor you should be able to recognize and explain. Connect it to the purpose of Security Control Types rather than memorizing the phrase by itself.
Evaluate risk and verify whether controls meet organizational, legal, or regulatory requirements.

course.check_a: Directive controls tell people what they are expected or required to do. Policies, procedures, standards, and mandatory training guide behavior. Key ideas include: Security policies and procedures; Training materials and awareness campaigns; Risk assessments and compliance audits.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Ensuring authorized users can access systems and data when needed.
Ensuring data stays accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized modification.
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability—the three foundational information-security objectives.
